claim: LRP16 expression was significantly higher in CRC tissue samples than adjacent normal tissues.
source: An analysis using the Image-Pro Plus software showed that the level of LRP16 expression was significantly higher in the CRC tissue samples than the adjacent normal tissues (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data from 202 CRC samples shown in Figure 1A-B, analyzed with Image-Pro Plus software.

claim: LRP16 was highly elevated in primary CRC tumors compared with their adjacent normal tissues as determined by RT-PCR and Western blot analysis.
source: LRP16 was highly elevated in primary CRC tumors compared with their adjacent normal tissues as determined by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and Western blot analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the histological grades of the tumors.
source: Notably, we found that the level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the histological grades of the tumors and was also strongly associated with a higher tumor stage (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by analysis of 202 CRC samples shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of LRP16 expression was strongly associated with a higher tumor stage.
source: Notably, we found that the level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the histological grades of the tumors and was also strongly associated with a higher tumor stage (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by analysis of tumor staging data from 202 CRC samples shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The level of LRP16 expression is progressively elevated during the progression of patients with CRC.
source: suggesting that the level of LRP16 expression is progressively elevated during the progression of the patients with CRC.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between LRP16 expression and tumor grades/stages shown in the data.

claim: A low level of LRP16 was associated with better overall survival (OS) in CRC patients (p=0.0224).
source: A Kaplan–Meier survival analysis of the expression of LRP16 and the clinical behavior of CRC further showed that a low level of LRP16 was associated with better overall survival (OS) in CRC patients (p=0.0224) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data from 202 CRC patients shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LRP16 expression was an independent prognostic factor, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.58 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36–0.90) in a multivariate analysis.
source: In this context, LRP16 expression was an independent prognostic factor, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.58 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36–0.90) in a multivariate analysis (tumor grades HR 0.46 [95% CI 0.26–0.82]; tumor stages HR 0.44 [95% CI 0.21–0.93]), which is similar to our previous findings (Xi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multivariate analysis of clinical data and cited previous findings from Xi et al., 2010.

claim: The expression of LRP16 transcripts is profoundly elevated in CRC according to The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database.
source: Interrogation of the most comprehensive public database, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012), also supported the notion that the expression of LRP16 transcripts is profoundly elevated in CRC.
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA database data cited from Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012.

claim: When CRC samples were stratified according to their tumor stage, the level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the clinical tumor stages (TNM stage) in TCGA database.
source: Interestingly, this database also showed that when CRC samples were further stratified according to their tumor stage, the level of LRP16 expression also positively correlated with the clinical tumor stages (TNM stage) of these patients with CRC (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: Supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the histological grades of CRC patients in TCGA database.
source: Further analysis of our data and the TCGA database showed that the level of LRP16 expression also positively correlated with the histological grades of these CRC patients
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA database and authors' own data.

claim: High levels of LRP16 expression in CRC strongly correlated with lymph-node positivity and metastasis.
source: and that, remarkably, high levels of LRP16 expression in CRC strongly correlated with lymph-node positivity and metastasis in the cohort of patients with CRC (Figure 1H–I and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of clinical data shown in Figure 1H-I and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Constitutive activation of NF-κB was observed in 28.7% (58 of 202) of the cohort of patients with CRC.
source: Constitutive activation of NF-κB was observed in 28.7% (58 of 202) of the cohort of patients with CRC (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data from 202 CRC samples shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The total p65 levels were significantly elevated in CRC samples compared with the adjacent normal tissues.
source: The total p65 levels slightly differed among the CRC samples, but they were significantly elevated in CRC samples compared with the adjacent normal tissues (Figure 1J)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Total p65 levels positively correlated with the histological grades of the tumors.
source: and also positively correlated with the histological grades of the tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the level of p65 expression.
source: An analysis of consecutive tissue sections showed that the level of LRP16 expression positively correlated with the level of p65 expression (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by analysis of consecutive tissue sections shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Approximately 66% of the samples with high LRP16 expression displayed high p65 expression.
source: Specifically, approximately 66% of the samples with high LRP16 expression displayed high p65 expression, whereas approximately 68% of the low LRP16 samples displayed low p65 expression (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of 202 samples shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Approximately 68% of the low LRP16 samples displayed low p65 expression.
source: Specifically, approximately 66% of the samples with high LRP16 expression displayed high p65 expression, whereas approximately 68% of the low LRP16 samples displayed low p65 expression (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of 202 samples shown in Figure 1L.

claim: The phosphorylation of p65 (phospho-p65) at Ser536 was significantly higher in CRC tissues.
source: Similar to the expression of LRP16, the phosphorylation of p65 (phospho-p65) at Ser536, which represents the activated form of NF-κB, was significantly higher in CRC tissues.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: High expression levels of phospho-p65 correlated positively with high expression levels of LRP16 in CRC clinical specimens.
source: Most importantly, high expression levles of phospho-p65 correlated positively with high expression levels of LRP16 in CRC clinical specimens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: XIAP expression was significantly elevated in all 202 CRC tissues compared with the adjacent normal tissues.
source: Informatively, XIAP (a target of NF-κB) expression was significantly elevated in all 202 CRC tissues compared with the adjacent normal tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no significant correlation between LRP16 and XIAP expression in CRC samples from the authors' cohort.
source: However, we did not observe a significant correlation between LRP16 and XIAP expression in these CRC samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LRP16 expression was not significantly correlated with that of BCL2L1 in the TCGA CRC RNA-seq dataset.
source: Moreover, analysis of the TCGA CRC RNA-seq dataset revealed that LRP16 expression was also not significantly correlated with that of BCL2L1 (anti-apoptotic transcriptional target of NF-κB), but it was inversely correlated to that of XIAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA CRC RNA-seq dataset shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LRP16 expression was inversely correlated to that of XIAP in the TCGA CRC RNA-seq dataset.
source: Moreover, analysis of the TCGA CRC RNA-seq dataset revealed that LRP16 expression was also not significantly correlated with that of BCL2L1 (anti-apoptotic transcriptional target of NF-κB), but it was inversely correlated to that of XIAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA CRC RNA-seq dataset shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LRP16 is overexpressed in human CRC samples compared with adjacent normal samples.
source: Taken together, these results provide overwhelming clinical evidence that LRP16 is overexpressed in human CRC samples compared with adjacent normal samples, and also confirms the critical role of LRP16 in promoting CRC tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data presented in Figure 1 and related supplements.

claim: LRP16 plays a critical role in promoting CRC tumorigenesis.
source: Taken together, these results provide overwhelming clinical evidence that LRP16 is overexpressed in human CRC samples compared with adjacent normal samples, and also confirms the critical role of LRP16 in promoting CRC tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation of LRP16 expression with tumor grades, stages, and survival outcomes.

claim: CRC cell lines expressing relatively higher levels of endogenous LRP16 were less sensitive to etoposide.
source: The results indicated that CRC cell lines (i.e. LS180, HCT116, and RKO) expressing relatively higher levels of endogenous LRP16 were less sensitive to etoposide.
evidence: Supported by IC50 measurements comparing different CRC cell lines with varying LRP16 expression levels, as mentioned in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CRC cell lines expressing relatively lower or undetectable levels of endogenous LRP16 were more sensitive to etoposide.
source: In contrast, CRC cell lines expressing relatively lower or undetectable levels of endogenous LRP16 (i.e. SW480, CaCO2, and LoVo) were more sensitive to etoposide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by IC50 measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Forced overexpression of LRP16 in SW480 cells rendered tumor cells more resistant to etoposide than to 5-fluorouracil or oxaliplatin.
source: As expected, the forced overexpression of LRP16 in SW480 cells with a basic low level of LRP16 rendered tumor cells more resistant to etoposide than to the other two drugs, as evidenced by increased cell viability and clonogenicity (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Increasing the expression of LRP16 substantially rescued etoposide-induced apoptosis.
source: Increasing the expression of LRP16 substantially rescued etoposide-induced apoptosis, as evidenced by reduced caspase three cleavage (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of caspase-3 cleavage shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LRP16 overexpression had no significant protective effects on the invasive and metastatic capacities of the CRC cell line ex vivo.
source: However, no significant protective effects were observed on the invasive and metastatic capacities of the CRC cell line ex vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by transwell invasion assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Elevated phospho-p65 levels were associated with substantially enhanced NF-κB transcriptional activity in etoposide non-responsive cell lines.
source: We found that elevated phospho-p65 levels, which were associated with substantially enhanced NF-κB transcriptional activity, occurred in the most etoposide non-responsive cell lines.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and transcriptional activity data mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In some etoposide-responsive cells, upregulation of the phospho-p65 level or NF-κB transcriptional activity did not remarkably occur.
source: Conversely, in some etoposide-responsive cells, upregulation of the phospho-p65 level or NF-κB transcriptional activity did not remarkably occur (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Gradual increase in LRP16 expression significantly increased the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of IKKα and IKKβ.
source: The Western blot results also showed that with a gradually increase in LRP16 expression significantly increased the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of the upstream regulators of the NF-κB pathway, IKKα and IKKβ, and also increased the levels of phospho-p65 (Figure 2E), compared with those in controls.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Gradual increase in LRP16 expression increased the levels of phospho-p65.
source: The Western blot results also showed that with a gradually increase in LRP16 expression significantly increased the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of the upstream regulators of the NF-κB pathway, IKKα and IKKβ, and also increased the levels of phospho-p65 (Figure 2E), compared with those in controls.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Gradual re-expression of exogenous LRP16 in SW480 cells restored their resistance to etoposide.
source: Similar results in clonogenicity experiments demonstrated that the gradual re-expression of exogenous LRP16 in SW480 cells restored their resistance to etoposide (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Blocking NF-κB activation with BAY 11-7082 in SW480 cells exogenously expressing LRP16 profoundly reduced their viability and clonogenicity.
source: Blocking NF-κB activation with either BAY 11–7082 or IκBαSR in SW480 cells exogenously expressing LRP16 or the vector control profoundly reduced their viability and clonogenicity (Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2F-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Blocking NF-κB activation with IκBαSR in SW480 cells exogenously expressing LRP16 profoundly reduced their viability and clonogenicity.
source: Blocking NF-κB activation with either BAY 11–7082 or IκBαSR in SW480 cells exogenously expressing LRP16 or the vector control profoundly reduced their viability and clonogenicity (Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2F-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: LRP16 confers DNA damage-triggered NF-κB-mediated expression of anti-apoptotic signaling molecules and is involved in restraining the response to DNA-damaging cytotoxic therapies in CRC cells.
source: These results suggest that LRP16 confers DNA damage-triggered NF-κB-mediated expression of anti-apoptotic signaling molecules and is involved in restraining the response to DNA-damaging cytotoxic therapies in CRC cells.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing LRP16's role in NF-κB activation and resistance to etoposide.

claim: Depletion of endogenous LRP16 resulted in significantly reduced cell viability and clonogenicity and profoundly enhanced the sensitivity of cells to etoposide.
source: Notably, depletion of endogenous LRP16 resulted in significantly reduced cell viability and clonogenicity and profoundly enhanced the sensitivity of cells to etoposide (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Ectopic expression of LRP16 mutants (D160A or I161A) in SW480 cells dramatically sensitized the tumor cells to genotoxic stress-induced apoptosis.
source: Of note, ectopic expression of LRP16 mutants (D160A or I161A), which was sufficient to significantly reduce its affinity for PAR, but not LRP16 wild-type (WT), in SW480 cells, dramatically sensitized the tumor cells to genotoxic stress-induced apoptosis, as conveyed by reduced cell viability and clonogenicity, in line with the indispensible role of the affinity of LRP16 for PAR in NF-κB activation and anti-apoptotic transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: PARP inhibition by PJ-34 or 3-AB treatment significantly reduced CRC cells survival and dramatically sensitized cancer cells to etoposide-induced cell death.
source: Consistently, PARP inhibition by PJ-34 or 3-AB treatment also significantly reduced CRC cells survival and dramatically sensitized cancer cells to etoposide-induced cell death, as evidenced by the reduced cell viability and clonogenicity, in LRP16-upregulated SW480 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: LRP16 plays a critical role in DNA-damage-initiated and PAR-dependent NF-κB transactivation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that LRP16 plays a critical role in DNA-damage-initiated and PAR-dependent NF-κB transactivation, which could account for the limited or lack of response to the cytotoxic and cytostatic effects of etoposide and protection against cell death induced by genotoxic agents.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing LRP16's PAR-binding requirement for NF-κB activation and drug resistance.

claim: Re-expression of LRP16 in cells exposed to etoposide profoundly increased the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of IKKα, IKKβ and IκBα, in a dose- and time-dependent manner.
source: The results indicated that the re-expression of LRP16 in cells exposed to etoposide profoundly increased the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of the upstream regulators of the NF-κB pathway, IKKα, IKKβ and IκBα, in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Exposure to IR, together with exogenous LRP16 expression, largely prolonged the IR-stimulated activation of NF-κB compared with cells transfected with control vector.
source: Consistent with this phenomenon, exposure to IR, together with exogenous LRP16 expression, also largely prolonged the IR-stimulated activation of NF-κB compared with that in cells transfected with control vector (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LRP16 deficiency introduced by its siRNAs in cells exposed to etoposide reduced the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of IKKα, IKKβ, and IκBα, in a dose- and time-dependent manner.
source: Conversely, LRP16 deficiency introduced by its siRNAs in cells exposed to etoposide reduced the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of IKKα, IKKβ, and IκBα, in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IR triggered the phosphorylation of IKKα, IKKβ, and p65, and IκBα was substantially reduced in SW620 cells expressing LRP16-specific siRNAs compared with those transfected with scrambled nonspecific siRNAs.
source: Consistent with these data, IR triggered the phosphorylation of IKKα, IKKβ, and p65, and IκBα was substantially reduced in SW620 cells expressing LRP16-specific siRNAs compared with those transfected with scrambled nonspecific siRNAs (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The nuclear accumulation of NF-κB/p65 was substantially reduced in the LRP16-specific siRNAs-transfected cell lysates compared with that in the controls.
source: Moreover, the nuclear accumulation of NF-κB/p65 was also substantially reduced in the LRP16-specific siRNAs-transfected cell lysates compared with that in the controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LRP16 is a key regulator of the DNA damage-stimulated activation of NF-κB.
source: Taken together, these results support the critical function of LRP16 in controlling the DNA damage-stimulated activation of NF-κB.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing LRP16's effects on NF-κB pathway components.

claim: Exogenous expression of LRP16 with a silent mutation at the shRNA target site rescued the effect of LRP16 siRNA on etoposide-triggered phosphorylation of IKKα, IKKβ, p65, and IκBα.
source: Our results showed that the etoposide-triggered phosphorylation of IKKα, IKKβ, p65, and IκBα was substantially reduced in the LRP16 siRNA_374-transfected cell lysates. Conversely, exogenous expression of LRP16 with a silent mutation at the shRNA target site rescued this effect (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Exogenous expression of LRP16 had almost no effect on the activation of NF-κB1 (noncanonical NF-κB signaling pathway) induced by etoposide.
source: However, our results also indicated that, compared with the control, the exogenous expression of LRP16 had almost no effect on the activation of NF-κB1 (noncanonical NF-κB signaling pathway) induced by etoposide (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: LRP16 is a key regulator of the activating phosphorylation of the activation loops of IKKs and hence of IKK function in the physiological context.
source: These data suggest that LRP16 is a key regulator of the activating phosphorylation of the activation loops of IKKs and hence of IKK function in the physiological context.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing LRP16's effects on IKK phosphorylation.

claim: The exogenous expression of LRP16 in SW480 cells did not induce significant phosphorylation of TAK1 compared with that in the control.
source: Unexpectedly, the exogenous expression of LRP16 in SW480 cells did not induce significant phosphorylation of TAK1 compared with that in the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Other upstream kinases could contribute to the activation of IKK mediated by LRP16 within the context of etoposide-induced NF-κB signal transduction.
source: raising the additional possibility that other upstream kinases could contribute to the activation of IKK mediated by LRP16 within the context of etoposide-induced NF-κB signal transduction.
evidence: Speculated based on the lack of TAK1 phosphorylation by LRP16.

claim: Ectopic expression of LRP16 WT, but not its mutants (D160A or I161A), significantly enhanced NF-κB activation after etoposide treatment.
source: Ectopic expression of LRP16 WT, but not its mutants (D160A or I161A), which were sufficient to significantly reduce its affinity to PAR (Wu et al., 2015), significantly enhanced NF-κB activation after etoposide treatment, as conveyed by the phosphorylated forms of IKKα and IKKβ, p65, and IκBα (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3F and cited previous work from Wu et al., 2015.

claim: Ectopic of LRP16 remarkably enhanced the levels of NF-κB-dependent luciferase reporter gene activity in both SW480 and LoVo cells following either etoposide or IR treatment.
source: Ectopic of LRP16 remarkably enhanced the levels of NF-κB-dependent luciferase reporter gene activity in both SW480 and LoVo cells following either etoposide or IR treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: LRP16 deficiency introduced by two siRNAs in both HCT116 and SW620 cells considerably diminished the NF-κB transcriptional activity in response to etoposide or IR.
source: Conversely, LRP16 deficiency introduced by two siRNAs in both HCT116 and SW620 cells considerably diminished the NF-κB transcriptional activity in response to etoposide or IR (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Ectopic expression of LRP16 WT, but not its mutants (D160A or I161A) dramatically enhanced the NF-κB transcriptional activity in response to etoposide or IR.
source: Of note, ectopic expression of LRP16 WT, but not its mutants (D160A or I161A) dramatically enhanced the NF-κB transcriptional activity in response to etoposide or IR (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: LRP16 controls DNA damage-initiated and PAR-dependent NF-κB signaling activation.
source: thus supporting the critical function of LRP16 in controlling DNA damage-initiated and PAR-dependent NF-κB signaling activation.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing LRP16's PAR-binding requirement for NF-κB activation.

claim: Cells exogenously expressing LRP16 in response to etoposide develop alterations of the global transcription profile.
source: The results indicate that cells exogenously expressing LRP16 in response to etoposide develop alterations of the global transcription profile (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Several pathways are highly affected by LRP16, including protein-K63-linked ubiquitination, IκB phosphorylation, and the DNA damage response.
source: Further pathway analysis has revealed several pathways that are highly affected by LRP16, including protein-K63-linked ubiquitination, IκB phosphorylation, and the DNA damage response (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: After exposure to etoposide, the expression of apoptosis-related genes was markedly downregulated in cells with exogenously expression of LRP16, compared with the control cells.
source: The results indicate that after exposure to etoposide, the expression of apoptosis-related genes was markedly downregulated, whereas the expression of anti-apoptosis-related genes was strikingly increased in cells with exogenously expression of LRP16, compared with the control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by PCR array data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: After exposure to etoposide, the expression of anti-apoptosis-related genes was strikingly increased in cells with exogenously expression of LRP16, compared with the control cells.
source: The results indicate that after exposure to etoposide, the expression of apoptosis-related genes was markedly downregulated, whereas the expression of anti-apoptosis-related genes was strikingly increased in cells with exogenously expression of LRP16, compared with the control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by PCR array data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: LRP16 is functionally involved in the NF-κB-dependent gene expression induced by etoposide stimulation.
source: These results suggest that LRP16 is functionally involved in the NF-κB-dependent gene expression induced by etoposide stimulation and might account for the compromised therapeutic efficacy of etoposide.
evidence: Inferred from the gene expression changes observed in LRP16-expressing cells after etoposide treatment.

claim: PKR potentially interacted with LRP16 according to LC-MS/MS data.
source: An in-depth bioinformatics analysis of the LC–MS/MS data indicated that PKR with the matching peptide potentially interacted with LRP16.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The interaction of endogenous LRP16 with PKR protein was confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation in SW480 cells after etoposide treatment.
source: Importantly, the interaction of endogenous LRP16 with PKR protein was confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) in SW480 cells after etoposide treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ethidium bromide did not markedly impair the etoposide-induced interaction between LRP16 and PKR, suggesting that this interaction was DNA-independent.
source: As expected, ethidium bromide did not markedly impair the etoposide-induced interaction between LRP16 and PKR, suggesting that this interaction was also DNA-independent (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with ethidium bromide shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The C-terminal catalytic domain of PKR mediated its physical interaction with LRP16.
source: A deletion analysis demonstrated that the C-terminal catalytic domain of PKR mediated its physical interaction with LRP16 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with PKR deletion mutants shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The macrodomain of LRP16 retained its ability to interact with PKR.
source: Figure 4E shows that the macrodomain of LRP16 retained is ability to interact with PKR.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with LRP16 deletion mutants shown in Figure 4E.

claim: GST pull-down assays using recombinant proteins demonstrated a direct LRP16–PKR interaction.
source: Our pull-down assays using the recombinant proteins demonstrated a direct LRP16–PKR interaction (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assay shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In vitro GST pull-down assays indicated that almost all PKR fragments, except ΔPKc, directly bound to LRP16.
source: Similarly, in vitro GST pull-down assays indicated that almost all PKR fragments, except ΔPKc, directly bound to LRP16.
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assays mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The ΔPKc-truncated PKR protein interacted negligibly with LRP16.
source: In contrast to the strong association between LRP16 and full-length PKR, the ΔPKc-truncated PKR protein interacted negligibly with LRP16 (Figure 4G)
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 4G.

claim: IKKβ with two matching peptides potentially interacted with LRP16 according to LC-MS/MS data.
source: Intriguingly, according to our LC–MS/MS data, IKKβ with two matching peptides potentially interacted with LRP16 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PKR binds specifically to the IKKβ subunit of the IKK complex and mediates the activation of NF-κB.
source: Consistent with this finding, previous studies have shown that PKR binds specifically to the IKKβ subunit of the IKK complex and mediates the activation of NF-κB (Bonnet et al., 2000; Zamanian-Daryoush et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Bonnet et al., 2000 and Zamanian-Daryoush et al., 2000.

claim: LRP16 was capable of interacting directly with both PKR and IKKβ, but independently with each.
source: The assay indicated that LRP16 was capable of interacting directly with both PKR and IKKβ, but independently with each (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assay shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Depletion of LRP16 introduced by its siRNAs resulted in the significant attenuation of the PKR–IKKβ interaction, both at baseline and after stimulation with etoposide.
source: Notably, depletion of LRP16 introduced by its siRNAs resulted in the significant attenuation of the PKR–IKKβ interaction, both at baseline and after stimulation with etoposide (Figure 4I)
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: LRP16 was required for the formation of a ternary complex with PKR and IKKβ.
source: suggesting that LRP16 was required for the formation of a ternary complex with PKR and IKKβ.
evidence: Inferred from the attenuation of PKR-IKKβ interaction upon LRP16 depletion.

claim: The interaction of endogenous LRP16 with the PKR protein was confirmed after etoposide treatment in TP53-null cells.
source: Unexpectedly, the interaction of endogenous LRP16 with the PKR protein was confirmed after etoposide treatment in TP53-null cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the interaction between the two proteins did not depend on the presence of p53 under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments in HCT116 p53-/- cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The interaction between LRP16 and PKR did not depend on the presence of p53.
source: Unexpectedly, the interaction of endogenous LRP16 with the PKR protein was confirmed after etoposide treatment in TP53-null cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the interaction between the two proteins did not depend on the presence of p53 under these conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LRP16-PKR interaction occurs in p53-null cells.

claim: Both endogenous and exogenous LRP16 dispersed from the nucleus to the cytosol after stimulation with etoposide, camptothecin, doxorubicin or IR.
source: After stimulation, both endogenous and exogenous LRP16 dispersed from the nucleus to the cytosol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy and subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The translocation of LRP16 was also detected after genotoxic stress in breast cancer and lung cancer cells.
source: More importantly, the translocation of LRP16 was also detected after genotoxic stress in other tumor cells, including breast cancer and lung cancer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In etoposide-treated cells, the interactions of both endogenous and exogenous LRP16 with PKR and IKKβ were observed and confirmed by co-IP only in cytoplasmic fractions, but they were negligible in the nuclear fractions.
source: As shown in Figure 4J and K, in the etoposide-treated cells, the interactions of both endogenous and exogenous LRP16 with PKR and IKKβ were observed and confirmed by co-IP only in cytoplasmic fractions, but they were negligible in the nuclear fractions.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: The overexpression of FLAG-tagged LRP16 in SW480 cells upon exposure to etoposide increased the interaction between PKR and IKKβ detected with co-IP, but only in the cytoplasmic fractions, with negligible effects in the nuclear fractions.
source: Notably, the overexpression of FLAG-tagged LRP16 in SW480 cells upon exposure to etoposide increased the interaction between PKR and IKKβ detected with co-IP, but only in the cytoplasmic fractions, with negligible effects in the nuclear fractions (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 4L.

claim: LRP16 plays an important role in the recruitment of PKR and IKKβ into a physical complex that facilitates the downstream signaling of NF-κB.
source: This finding suggests that LRP16 plays an important role in the recruitment of PKR and IKKβ into a physical complex that facilitates the downstream signaling of NF-κB.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LRP16 overexpression increases PKR-IKKβ interaction in the cytoplasm.

claim: The IR and/or etoposide-induced shift of LRP16 into the cytoplasmic complex fractions was completely blocked both by PARP inhibitors (3-AB or PJ-34) and by the PAR-binding-deficient mutant LRP16_I161A.
source: The IR and/or etoposide-induced shift of LRP16 into the cytoplasmic complex fractions was completely blocked both by PARP inhibitors (3-AB or PJ-34) and by the PAR-binding-deficient mutant LRP16_I161A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The translocation of LRP16 to the cytoplasm strictly depends on the presence of PAR and the intact PAR-binding motifs in LRP16.
source: suggesting that this process strictly depends on the presence of PAR and the intact PAR-binding motifs in LRP16.
evidence: Inferred from the blocking of LRP16 translocation by PARP inhibitors and PAR-binding-deficient mutants.

claim: Upon the detection of DNA lesions and PAR, LRP16 assembles the PKR and IKKβ complex in the cytoplasm.
source: Our data suggest that upon the detection of DNA lesions and PAR, LRP16 assembles the PKR and IKKβ complex in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing LRP16's PAR-dependent translocation and interaction with PKR and IKKβ in the cytoplasm.

claim: The PAR chains bound to LRP16 act as an interaction platform, which is required for PKR-mediated IKK activation and the activation of the NF-κB pathway in response to DNA damage.
source: The PAR chains bound to LRP16 act as an interaction platform, which is required for PKR-mediated IKK activation and the activation of the NF-κB pathway in response to DNA damage.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of PAR-binding for LRP16's function in NF-κB activation.

claim: The level of PKR expression was significantly elevated in the carcinoma tissues relative to that in the adjacent tissues.
source: Analysis of these data showed that the level of PKR expression was significantly elevated in the carcinoma tissues relative to that in the adjacent tissues (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data from 202 CRC samples shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PKR was highly elevated in primary CRC tumors compared with their adjacent normal tissues as determined by RT-PCR and Western blot analysis.
source: Moreover, PKR was highly elevated in primary CRC tumors compared with their adjacent normal tissues as determined by RT-PCR and Western blot analysis
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PKR expression positively correlated with the histological grades of the CRC patients.
source: and, noticeably, also positively correlated with the histological grades of the CRC patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which is consistent with the previous study (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and cited previous study by Kim et al., 2002.

claim: LRP16 expression positively correlated with PKR expression in consecutive tissue sections.
source: Further analysis of consecutive tissue sections showed that LRP16 expression positively correlated with PKR expression.
evidence: Supported by analysis of consecutive tissue sections mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 75% of the samples with high LRP16 expression also displayed high PKR expression.
source: Specifically, approximately 75% of the samples with high LRP16 expression also displayed high PKR expression, and approximately 58% of the low LRP16 samples displayed low PKR expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of 202 samples shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 58% of the low LRP16 samples displayed low PKR expression.
source: Specifically, approximately 75% of the samples with high LRP16 expression also displayed high PKR expression, and approximately 58% of the low LRP16 samples displayed low PKR expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of 202 samples shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Chemotherapeutic drugs, especially etoposide, activated PKR in CRC cell lines.
source: Chemotherapeutic drugs, especially etoposide, activated PKR in CRC cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Cells ectopically expressing LRP16 profoundly enhanced the PKR activity induced by etoposide in a time- and dose dependent manner.
source: Cells ectopically expressing LRP16 profoundly enhanced the PKR activity induced by etoposide in a time- and dose dependent manner (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LRP16 depletion introduced by its siRNAs dramatically blocked the etoposide-induced activation of PKR.
source: Conversely, LRP16 depletion introduced by its siRNAs dramatically blocked the etoposide-induced activation of PKR (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon exposure to etoposide, the introduction of LRP16 WT, but not its mutants LRP16_D160A or LRP16_I161A, profoundly increased the activation of PKR.
source: Upon exposure to etoposide, the introduction of LRP16 WT, but not its mutants LRP16_D160A or LRP16_I161A, profoundly increased the activation of PKR, as evidenced by the level of its autophosphorylation, without affecting its total protein level (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The PAR-binding activity of LRP16 is required for the DNA-damage-induced PKR activity.
source: suggesting that the PAR-binding activity of LRP16 is also required for the DNA-damage-induced PKR activity.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of intact PAR-binding motifs for LRP16 to enhance PKR activation.

claim: Knockdown of PKR introduced by its siRNAs reduced the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of IKKα and IKKβ, which are induced by LRP16 upon exposure to etoposide.
source: Western blot analysis showed that knockdown of PKR introduced by its siRNAs reduced the phosphorylated forms, but not the total forms, of the upstream regulators of the NF-κB pathway, IKKα and IKKβ, which are induced by LRP16 upon exposure to etoposide (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Knockdown of PKR impaired the interaction between LRP16 and IKKβ after etoposide treatment.
source: and also impaired the interaction between LRP16 and IKKβ after etoposide treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PKR acts as an adaptor protein and may be critical for the LRP16-mediated activation of IKK in response to DNA damage.
source: suggesting that PKR acts as an adaptor protein and may be critical for the LRP16-mediated activation of IKK in response to DNA damage.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of PKR for LRP16-mediated IKK activation and LRP16-IKKβ interaction.

claim: Depletion of PKR significantly abrogated the activation of NF-κB mediated by LRP16 upon IR stimulation.
source: Similarly, upon IR stimulation, depletion of PKR significantly abrogated the activation of NF-κB mediated by LRP16 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The etoposide-induced activation of IKK kinases was significantly reduced in the absence of either LRP16 or PKR expression.
source: Noticeably, the etoposide-induced activation of IKK kinases was significantly reduced in the absence of either LRP16 or PKR expression (Figure 5H)
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The formation and integration of the ternary complex containing LRP16, PKR, and IKK kinases plays a crucial role in the DNA-damage-induced transactivation of NF-κB.
source: suggesting that the formation and integration of the ternary complex containing LRP16, PKR, and IKK kinases plays a crucial role in the DNA-damage-induced transactivation of NF-κB.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of both LRP16 and PKR for IKK activation.

claim: The effect of LRP16 overexpression on the resistance of CRC cells to etoposide was offset, at least in part, when PKR was simultaneously depleted.
source: The results of cell viability and clonogenicity assays showed that the effect of LRP16 overexpression on the resistance of CRC cells to etoposide was offset, at least in part, when PKR was simultaneously depleted (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knocking down PKR in cells expressing LRP16 re-sensitized the cells to etoposide-induced DNA damage.
source: Similarly, knocking down PKR in cells expressing LRP16 re-sensitized the cells to etoposide-induced DNA damage, when measured by Annexin-V/PI binding assay.
evidence: Supported by Annexin-V/PI binding assay mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Knocking down PKR in cells expressing LRP16 was accompanied by elevated level of caspase three cleavage.
source: Meanwhile, this phenomenon was accompanied by elevated level of caspase three cleavage (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The inhibition of PKR catalytic activity with 2-aminopurine (2-AP) had no significant effect on the activation of IKK induced by LRP16 after DNA damage.
source: Notably, the inhibition of PKR catalytic activity with the chemical inhibitor 2-aminopurine (2-AP) had no significant effect on the activation of IKK induced by LRP16 after DNA damage (e.g. etoposide or IR) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: 2-aminopurine (2-AP) markedly inhibited the phosphorylation of IκBα.
source: but it markedly inhibited the phosphorylation of IκBα (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: PKR activates IKK via a direct protein–protein interaction, possibly via the IKKβ subunit, rather than by its kinase activity.
source: These data together demonstrate that PKR activates IKK via a direct protein–protein interaction, possibly via the IKKβ subunit, rather than by its kinase activity.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of PKR kinase inhibitor on IKK activation and the requirement of PKR for LRP16-IKKβ interaction.

claim: LRP16 activates the NF-κB signaling pathway via its interaction with and activation of PKR, which acts as an adaptor protein and activates IKK complexes in response to DNA-damaging cytotoxic therapies.
source: Thus, LRP16 activates the NF-κB signaling pathway via its interaction with and activation of PKR, which acts as an adaptor protein and activates IKK complexes in response to DNA-damaging cytotoxic therapies.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing LRP16's interaction with PKR, PKR's role in IKK activation, and the effects on drug resistance.

claim: MRS2578 and NECA were identified as competitive inhibitors of the affinity of LRP16 for PAR.
source: Among these small molecules, two compounds, MRS2578 (C20H20N5S4, molecular weight [MW] 472.67), a potent P2Y6 receptor antagonist (Syhr et al., 2014), and NECA (C12H16N6O4, MW 308.29), a potent adenosine receptor agonist (Ye et al., 2016), were identified as competitive inhibitors of the affinity of LRP16 for PAR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by PAR-binding assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and cited previous studies by Syhr et al., 2014 and Ye et al., 2016.

claim: IKKβ kinase activity was markedly attenuated in IR-stimulated cells pretreated with MRS2578, NECA, 3-AB, or PJ-34 compared with that in IR-stimulated control cells.
source: Accordingly, we found that IKKβ kinase activity was markedly attenuated in IR-stimulated cells pretreated with these two compounds or the PARP inhibitors 3-AB and PJ-34 (used as positive controls) compared with that in IR-stimulated control cells.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The inhibition of IKKβ kinase activity by NECA was less efficient than MRS2578.
source: However, the inhibition of IKKβ kinase activity by NECA was less efficient than MRS2578 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MRS2578 limited the activation of NF-κB induced by DNA damage.
source: Therefore, the small molecule MRS2578 conformed to our requirements and limited the activation of NF-κB induced by DNA damage.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of MRS2578 to inhibit IKKβ kinase activity.

claim: MRS2578 treatment for 24 hr markedly and dose-dependently reduced the viability of CRC cell lines.
source: As indicated in Figure 6A, MRS2578 treatment for 24 hr markedly and dose-dependently reduced the viability of the CRC cell lines.
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A significantly lower percentage of EdU-incorporated (proliferating) cells was observed in the MRS2578-treated cells than in the control cells.
source: Consistent with this finding, a significantly lower percentage of 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU)-incorporated (proliferating) cells was observed in the MRS2578-treated cells than in the control cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling assay shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MRS2578 markedly suppressed the proliferation in the CRC cells, as evidenced by their reduced clonogenic survival.
source: MRS2578 also markedly suppressed the proliferation in the CRC cells, as evidenced by their reduced clonogenic survival (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by clonogenic survival assays shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MRS2578 inhibits the survival and proliferation of CRC cells in vitro.
source: Collectively, these data show that MRS2578 inhibits the survival and proliferation of CRC cells in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing MRS2578's effects on cell viability, proliferation, and clonogenicity.

claim: Etoposide-induced activation of NF-κB was significantly and dose-dependently inhibited when cells were pretreated with MRS2578.
source: Of note, etoposide-induced the activation of NF-κB, as judged by the phosphorylation forms of IKKα and IKKβ, p65, and IκBα, but not the total form, was significantly and dose-dependently inhibited when cells were pretreated with MRS2578 (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CRC pretreated with MRS2578 induces cell killing and abrogates LRP16-mediated NF-κB activation in response to etoposide, leading to conversion of LRP16 from a survival into a killer molecule.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that CRC pretreated with MRS2578 induces cell killing and abrogates LRP16-mediated NF-κB activation in response to etoposide, leading to conversion of LRP16 from a survival into a killer molecule.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing MRS2578's effects on cell killing and NF-κB inhibition.

claim: Both SW480 and HCT116 cells treated with the combination of etoposide and MRS2578 showed synergistic cytotoxicity when assessed with the CalcuSyn model.
source: Of note, both SW480 and HCT116 cells treated with the combination of the two drugs showed synergistic cytotoxicity when assessed with the CalcuSyn model (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by combination index analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cells stably overexpressing LRP16 displayed less sensitivity to etoposide alone than control cells, but these cells were even more sensitive to a combination of etoposide and MRS2578.
source: Cells stably overexpressing LRP16 displayed less sensitivity to etoposide alone than control cells, but these cells were even more sensitive to a combination of etoposide and MRS2578 (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and clonogenicity assays shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The protection against apoptosis afforded by LRP16 overexpression in response to etoposide was offset, at least partially, when MRS2578 was used simultaneously.
source: Notably, the protection against apoptosis afforded by LRP16 overexpression in response to etoposide was offset, at least partially, when MRS2578 was used stimultaneously (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by Annexin-V/PI binding assay shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Both cells stably expressing LRP16 and the control pretreated with MRS2578 displayed significant reductions in the proportions of cells in G0/G1 phase and showed significantly increased in the percentages of the cells in G2 phase.
source: Additionally, results from cell-cycle profiling revealed that both cells stably expressing LRP16 and the control pretreated with MRS2578 displayed significant reductions in the proportions of cells in G0/G1 phase and showed significantly increased in the percentages of the cells in G2 phase (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: MRS2578 increases the sensitivity of CRC cells to etoposide by enhancing their apoptosis and inhibiting cell growth.
source: These findings reveal that MRS2578 increases the sensitivity of CRC cells to etoposide by enhancing their apoptosis and inhibiting cell growth.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing MRS2578's effects on apoptosis and cell cycle.

claim: Compared with their parental cells, both the DLD1_R and HT-29_R cells were substantially sensitized to MRS2578.
source: Compared with their parental cells, both the DLD1_R and HT-29_R cells were substantially sensitized to MRS2578 (Figure 6J)
evidence: Supported by cell viability assays shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The cytostatic effect of MRS2578 contributed to increasing the sensitivity or reducing the resistance of the cells to IR, and the cytostatic effect was independent of the IR resistance mechanism.
source: indicating that the cytostatic effect of MRS2578 (by inducing apoptosis and reducing cell growth) contributed to increasing the sensitivity or reducing the resistance of the cells to IR, and that the cytostatic effect was also independent of the IR resistance mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IR-resistant cells are sensitized to MRS2578.

claim: Cells pretreated with MRS2578 significantly impeded the phosphorylation of IKKα and IKKβ induced by etoposide, similar to the phenomenon detected in cells stably expressing D160A and I161A.
source: Of note, cells pretreated with MRS2578 significantly impeded the phosphorylation of IKKα and IKKβ induced by etoposide, similar to the phenomenon detected in cells stably expressing D160A and I161A (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pretreating cells with MRS2578 profoundly reduced both the etoposide-stimulated phosphorylation of IKKα and IKKβ and the etoposide-stimulated autophosphorylation of PKR.
source: Pretreating cells with MRS2578 profoundly reduced both the etoposide-stimulated phosphorylation of IKKα and IKKβ and the etoposide-stimulated autophosphorylation of PKR (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6K.

claim: MRS2578 inhibited the etoposide-stimulated interaction among LRP16, PKR, and IKKβ and thus prevented the formation of a ternary complex.
source: Furthermore, it also inhibited the etoposide-stimulated interaction among LRP16, PKR, and IKKβ and thus prevented the formation of a ternary complex, which might eventually impede the PKR activation of IKK (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Inhibiting the binding of LRP16 to PAR or pretreating cells with MRS 2578 is as effective as inhibiting PKR activity in blocking the biochemical effects of PKR in the cytoplasm and in inhibiting the NF-κB activity induced by LRP16 in response to DNA damage.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that inhibiting the binding of LRP16 to PAR or pretreating cells with MRS 2578 is as effective as inhibiting PKR activity in blocking the biochemical effects of PKR in the cytoplasm and in inhibiting the NF-κB activity induced by LRP16 in response to DNA damage.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data showing MRS2578's effects on PKR and IKK activation.

claim: Stable knockdown of LRP16 introduced by its shRNAs in SW620 cells suppressed tumor growth in the subcutaneous xenograft model.
source: Stable knockdown of LRP16 introduced by its shRNAs in SW620 cells suppressed tumor growth in the subcutaneous xenograft model.
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The mean weight of LRP16-silenced tumors was reduced in SW620 cells compared with controls.
source: The mean weight of LRP16-silenced tumors was also reduced in SW620 cells compared with controls (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by tumor weight measurements shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Stable knockdown of LRP16 was associated with a significant reduction in the growth of the primary SW620 tumors and a marked increase in the sensitivity of the xenograft tumors to etoposide treatment.
source: Of note, compared with controls, stable knockdown of LRP16 was not only associated with a significant reduction in the growth of the primary SW620 tumors, but also with a marked increase in the sensitivity of the xenograft tumors to etoposide treatment (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume and weight measurements shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of LRP16 significantly inhibited cell proliferation and sensitized tumor cells to etoposide in SW620 cell xenograft models, as determined by Ki-67 staining.
source: Knockdown of LRP16 significantly inhibited cell proliferation and sensitized tumor cells to etoposide in SW620 cell xenograft models, as determined by Ki-67 staining.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SW620 xenografts stably expressing shLRP16 showed the induction of apoptosis following etoposide treatment, as evidenced by the increased expression of TUNEL.
source: SW620 xenografts stably expressing shLRP16 showed the induction of apoptosis following etoposide treatment, as evidenced by the increased expression of terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The expression of LRP16 is not only required, but also sufficient to promote radio-resistance in a CRC tumor model.
source: Similar results were also obtained after IR treatment of the mouse xenograft tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–E), indicating that the expression of LRP16 is not only required, but also sufficient to promote radio-resistance in a CRC tumor model.
evidence: Supported by xenograft experiments with IR treatment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: Knockdown of LRP16 is synthetically lethal in CRC in vivo through suppressing cell growth and sensitizing the tumor to genotoxicity therapies.
source: Collectively, knockdown of LRP16 is synthetically lethal in CRC in vivo through suppressing cell growth and sensitizing the tumor to genotoxicity therapies.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative in vivo data showing LRP16 knockdown effects on tumor growth and drug sensitivity.

claim: Treatment of mice with MRS2578 resulted in a dose-dependent repression of CRC in vivo.
source: The results showed that treatment of mice with MRS2578 resulted in a dose-dependent repression of CRC in vivo (Figure 7Ca–Cb).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume and weight measurements shown in Figure 7Ca-Cb.

claim: The number of cells was substantially reduced in the tumors treated with MRS2578, and the tumors were filled with fibrosis-like tissue.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of the tumor tissues showed that the number of cells was substantially reduced in the tumors treated with MRS2578, and that the tumors were filled with fibrosis-like tissue.
evidence: Supported by H&E staining mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 7Cc.

claim: The expression of Ki67 was profoundly reduced in the tumor cells treated with MRS2578.
source: Consistent with this finding, an IHC analysis indicated that the expression of Ki67 was profoundly reduced in the tumor cells treated with MRS2578 (Figure 7Cc).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7Cc.

claim: No significant weight loss or organ toxicities were observed in the mice treated with MRS2578.
source: No significant weight loss or organ toxicities were observed in the mice treated with MRS2578 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3Aa–Ab).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements and H&E staining of organs shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3Aa-Ab.

claim: Doses between 10 and 20 mg/kg provide the optimal therapeutic index for MRS2578 for in vivo experimentation involving CRC xenografts.
source: These findings suggest that doses between 10 and 20 mg/kg provide the optimal therapeutic index for MRS2578 for in vivo experimentation involving CRC xenografts.
evidence: Inferred from the efficacy and toxicity data at different doses.

claim: Mice treated with etoposide alone showed a significant reduction in tumor burden versus those treated with vehicle alone.
source: First, for SW620 cells xenografts, as expected, mice treated with etoposide alone showed a significant reduction in tumor burden versus those treated with vehicle alone.
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 7Da-Db.

claim: The combination treatment of etoposide and MRS2578 yielded a further tumor burden reduction compared with vehicle or etoposide alone.
source: However, the combination (simultaneous drug administration) treatment yielded a further tumor burden reduction compared with vehicle or etoposide alone (Figure 7Da–Db and Figure 7—figure supplement 3Ba–Bb).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 7Da-Db and Figure 7—figure supplement 3Ba-Bb.

claim: No significant weight loss and no organ toxicities were observed in mice that received combination treatment of etoposide and MRS2578 throughout the study.
source: The treatment was well tolerated, as no significant weight loss and no organ toxicities were observed in mice that received these treatments, including combined treatment, throughout the study (Figure 7—figure supplement 3Ba–Bb).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements and H&E staining of organs shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3Ba-Bb.

claim: The combination of etoposide and MRS2578 resulted in significantly greater growth inhibition, as determined by Ki-67 staining.
source: Of note, the combination of etoposide and MRS2578 resulted in significantly greater growth inhibition, as determined by Ki-67 staining (Figure 7Dc).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7Dc.

claim: Phospho-p65 levels, but not total forms, are clearly decreased in the compound MRS2578 treated groups in xenograft tumors.
source: As expected, phospho-p65 levels, but not total forms, are clearly decreased in the compound MRS2578 treated groups (Figure 7Dd).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of tumor lysates shown in Figure 7Dd.

claim: Treatment with the combination of etoposide and MRS2578 further reduced tumor growth in CT26 colorectal adenocarcinomas implanted into BALB/c mice.
source: As expected, treatment with the combination of etoposide and MRS2578 further reduced tumor growth, indicating that this combination was more active than either single agent alone in inhibiting CRC cell growth and significantly prolonged mouse survival (Figure 7E–F and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements and survival analysis shown in Figure 7E-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The combination of etoposide and MRS2578 significantly prolonged mouse survival in CT26 colorectal adenocarcinomas implanted into BALB/c mice.
source: As expected, treatment with the combination of etoposide and MRS2578 further reduced tumor growth, indicating that this combination was more active than either single agent alone in inhibiting CRC cell growth and significantly prolonged mouse survival (Figure 7E–F and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: There were no significant reductions in the mouse bodyweights in the combination treatment group, indicating that the toxicity of this combination is controllable.
source: There were no significant reductions in the mouse bodyweights, indicating that the toxicity of this combination is controllable (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Pharmacologically targeting LRP16/NF-κB signaling prevents tumorigenesis.
source: Taken together, these findings show that pharmacologically targeting LRP16/NF-κB signaling prevents tumorigenesis and suggest that the combination of MRS2578 and etoposide offers therapeutic opportunities for CRC and may warrant an immediate clinical trial.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative in vivo data showing the effects of MRS2578 and combination therapy.

claim: The combination of MRS2578 and etoposide offers therapeutic opportunities for CRC and may warrant an immediate clinical trial.
source: Taken together, these findings show that pharmacologically targeting LRP16/NF-κB signaling prevents tumorigenesis and suggest that the combination of MRS2578 and etoposide offers therapeutic opportunities for CRC and may warrant an immediate clinical trial.
evidence: Speculated based on the promising preclinical results in xenograft models.

claim: LRP16 has a dual function in activating NF-κB: providing lesion specificity during DNA damage response and assembling the PKR and IKKβ complex in the cytoplasm.
source: Our previous and present studies favor two possible roles of LRP16 in activating NF-κB (Figure 8): first, LRP16 functions not only by providing the lesion specificity during the cellular response to DNA damage by its unique interactions with Ku70/Ku80, but also ensures the successful PARP1/PAR-dependent recruitment of both ATM and PIASy, together with NEMO. These results underscore the function of LRP16, a versatile protein that preferentially occurs in the nucleus, in the early nuclear signaling cascade following DNA damage; second, when LRP16 detects DNA lesions and PAR, it assembles the PKR and IKKβ complex, the key players in NF-κB activation, in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative data presented in the study and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: LRP16 appears to have a dual function, which might at least partially explain how DNA-damage-initiated nuclear events are linked to the activation of cytoplasmic IKK.
source: Thus, LRP16 appears to have a dual function, which might at least partially explain how these DNA-damage-initiated nuclear events are linked to the activation of cytoplasmic IKK.
evidence: Inferred from the dual roles of LRP16 in nuclear and cytoplasmic NF-κB signaling.

claim: Rates of tumor cell repopulation have been shown to accelerate in the intervals between successive courses of treatment.
source: Interestingly, rates of tumor cell repopulation have been shown to accelerate in the intervals between successive courses of treatment and solid tumors commonly show initial responses followed by rapid regrowth and subsequent resistance to further chemotherapy.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: Solid tumors commonly show initial responses followed by rapid regrowth and subsequent resistance to further chemotherapy.
source: Interestingly, rates of tumor cell repopulation have been shown to accelerate in the intervals between successive courses of treatment and solid tumors commonly show initial responses followed by rapid regrowth and subsequent resistance to further chemotherapy.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: The NF-κB signaling pathway has emerged as an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage.
source: The NF-κB signaling pathway has emerged as an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage, in particular NF-κB-conferred anti-apoptotic transcription facilitates the escape of cells from the lethal effects of DNA damage (Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Wu et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Wu et al., 2006.

claim: NF-κB-conferred anti-apoptotic transcription facilitates the escape of cells from the lethal effects of DNA damage.
source: The NF-κB signaling pathway has emerged as an important mediator for cellular responses to DNA damage, in particular NF-κB-conferred anti-apoptotic transcription facilitates the escape of cells from the lethal effects of DNA damage (Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Wu et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Janssens et al., 2005; Perkins, 2007; Wu et al., 2006.

claim: NF-κB initiates cell cycle checkpoint control to promote cellular recovery from damage.
source: and initiates cell cycle checkpoint control to promote cellular recovery from damage (McCool and Miyamoto, 2012; Miyamoto, 2011), thereby contributing to acquired resistance to DNA-damaging cytotoxic therapies.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by McCool and Miyamoto, 2012; Miyamoto, 2011.

claim: PARP1 was revealed to be indispensable for the signaling cascade that links nuclear DNA damage recognition to cytoplasmic IKK activation.
source: Besides NEMO (also named IKKγ) and ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), two known crucial regulators of the genotoxic stress-activated NF-κB signaling pathway (Miyamoto, 2011), poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) was recently revealed to be indispensable for the signaling cascade that links nuclear DNA damage recognition to cytoplasmic IKK activation (Stilmann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Miyamoto, 2011 and Stilmann et al., 2009.

claim: LRP16 was identified as a PAR-binding protein in genotoxic threat-treated cells and a putative substrate of PARP1.
source: Leukemia-Related Protein 16 (LRP16), a member of the macro domain family, was identified as a PAR-binding protein in genotoxic threat-treated cells and a putative substrate of PARP1, which suggests that LRP16 could be an important molecule in the cellular response to DNA damage (Han et al., 2011; Timinszky et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Han et al., 2011 and Timinszky et al., 2009.

claim: LRP16 facilitates the lesion-specific recruitment of PARP-1 and NEMO through its constitutive interactions with these two proteins.
source: Mechanistically, LRP16 facilitates the lesion-specific recruitment of PARP-1 and NEMO through its constitutive interactions with these two proteins, and then ultimately facilitates the concomitant recruitment of ATM and protein inhibitor of activated STAT Y (PIASy) to NEMO to ensure the activation of NF-κB after the induction of DSBs (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Wu et al., 2015.

claim: PKR has been implicated in the regulation or modulation of cell growth through multiple signaling pathways.
source: The double-stranded-RNA (dsRNA)-activated protein kinase PKR, a ubiquitously expressed serine/threonine kinase, has been implicated in the regulation or modulation of cell growth through multiple signaling pathways and has also been described as a signal integrator in the translational and transcriptional control pathways (Bennett et al., 2006; Dar et al., 2005; Donzé et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Bennett et al., 2006; Dar et al., 2005; Donzé et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: PKR has a role in signal transduction and transcriptional control through the IκB/NF-κB pathways.
source: In addition to its functional regulatory function, PKR has a role in signal transduction and transcriptional control through the IκB/NF-κB pathways (Gil et al., 2000, Gil et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Gil et al., 2000 and Gil et al., 2004.

claim: PKR specifically interacts with STATs, FADD, and IKK.
source: Investigators have shown that PKR specifically interacts with STATs, FADD, and IKK (Williams, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Williams, 2001.

claim: PKR has a novel role as a mediator of IR resistance, modulated partly by the protective effects of NF-κB activation.
source: and researchers have also described a novel role for PKR as a mediator of IR resistance, modulated partly by the protective effects of NF-κB activation (von Holzen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by von Holzen et al., 2007.

claim: Chemotherapeutic drugs such as doxorubicin, etoposide, and 5-fluorouracil are able to induce and activate PKR protein, triggering apoptosis.
source: Chemotherapeutic drugs such as doxorubicin, etoposide, and 5-fluorouracil are able to induce and activate PKR protein, triggering apoptosis (García et al., 2011; Peidis et al., 2011; Yoon et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by García et al., 2011; Peidis et al., 2011; Yoon et al., 2009.
